catalog_quote: Stress rule 1 ... i.e., all nouns, verbs, and adjectives receive a stress and pitch on the first two syllables. ... Stress Rule 1 provides the proper tone contour for words that do not have a closed second syllable. 'šón'táko 'young girl' 'čí'číka 'knife' 'má'pó 'head' However, the stress on the second syllable must be removed in these case, and words with a closed second syllable must be modified so that the initial syllable has no pitch or stress. Stress Rule 2 ... i.e., the initial syllabic of words which are monosyllabic or which have a closed second syllable becomes unstressed and "minus" for pitch, and any syllable which is preceded by a stressed syllabic becomes unstressed. ... sweep_summary: Capanahua is in the catalog as weight-sensitive (weight-sensitive with a fixed default: stress on the second syllable if closed by a non-glottal consonant, else initial; Loos 1969 ch. VII, read from page scan by the qs-tier). Three title items: (1) Elias-Ulloa 2006 dissertation, already held by the project, read: confirms the primary rule with fieldwork-backed disyllabic footing, and refines the weight class — long-vowel second syllables also take the head ((ka.ˈpiː) 'crocodile', (ra.ˈbiː).bi 'both', p.173), while closed odd syllables are light (p.179); secondary feet iterate. (2) Safir 1979 (MITWPL 1:95-114): no open copy found anywhere; per Hagberg 1993 it re-analyses Loos's data and is the source of the iterative secondary-stress coding; priority medium. (3) Hagberg 1993/2006 dissertation: downloaded from archive.org (new file), sec. 4.2 pp.212-215 gives a second-hand summary of Loos 1969 ('Stress occurs on the second syllable if it is closed (i.e., heavy), otherwise it falls on the first syllable'; monosyllables unstressed) — confirms. Two further on-disk sources read: Elias-Ulloa 2021 (Languages 6:158, first-hand, explicit two-syllable-window statement — the best new statement; confirms) and González 2017 (Amerindia 39, secondary survey; refines: heavy = coda, long vowel or nasalized vowel). Nothing supersedes Loos 1969 as the deciding source, but the catalog's 'no vowel-length criterion' should be annotated: Elias-Ulloa's data show CVː second syllables attracting stress.

new_statements.reading: A first-hand fieldworker's explicit statement: weight-sensitive stress in a two-syllable left window, peninitial iff the second syllable is closed, else initial, with high pitch on the stressed syllable. It matches the catalog's weight-sensitive with a fixed default 'peninitial if heavy else initial' coding from Loos 1969 exactly. Elias-Ulloa 2006 p.173 (also read, page scan) adds that a long second-syllable vowel likewise takes the head ((ka.ˈpiː) 'crocodile', (ra.ˈbiː).bi 'both'), so 'heavy' should be read as CVC-or-CVː rather than the catalog's 'no vowel-length criterion' (which is faithful to Loos 1969 alone), and p.179 states that closed odd syllables are light (a closed initial syllable never draws stress off an initial default).

new_statements.quote: p.15: "Cuando la segunda sílaba de una palabra termina con una oclusiva (se consideran a las nasales como oclusivas), la sílaba es acentuada." p.19: "ACENTUACIÓN. Cuando los afijos y raíces forman una palabra cuya segunda sílaba es cerrada, esa segunda sílaba lleva el acento. Por ejemplo, jisi (a ver) no lleva acento en la segunda sílaba porque la segunda es sílaba abierta. En cambio, jismís derivado de jis-mis (ver-tendencia: mirón) lleva acento porque la segunda sílaba es cerrada [...] Después de asignar el acento se suprimen las consonantes oclusivas que cierran una sílaba. [...] Es importante notar que el acento se preserva aunque la consonante se suprima. [...] mapéti, diferente de mapeti de mapet-i (subir-para: para subir) sin acento en la segunda sílaba."
new_statements.translation: p.15: "When the second syllable of a word ends in a stop (nasals are counted as stops), that syllable is stressed." p.19: "STRESS. When affixes and roots form a word whose second syllable is closed, that second syllable carries the stress. For example, jisi 'to see' does not carry stress on the second syllable because the second syllable is open. By contrast jismís, derived from jis-mis (see-tendency: 'onlooker'), carries stress because the second syllable is closed [...] After stress is assigned, the stops that close a syllable are deleted. [...] It is important to note that the stress is preserved even though the consonant is deleted. [...] mapéti, different from mapeti from mapet-i (climb-for: 'in order to climb') with no stress on the second syllable."

new_statements.relation_note: Same rule as Loos 1969 (the catalog source) and Elias-Ulloa 2021: closed second syllable takes the stress, otherwise not; the dictionary is the popular-orthography restatement of Loos's own analysis. It adds that the closing consonant may be an underlying stop or nasal later deleted (stress preserved), and it says nothing about long vowels attracting stress (Elias-Ulloa 2006's CVː refinement is neither confirmed nor denied; the orthography has no vowel length). It leaves the elsewhere-default (initial stress) implicit.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress goes to the second syllable of the word when that syllable is closed by a (surface or underlying) stop or nasal; when the second syllable is open, it is not stressed (the dictionary marks stress only in that peninitial-closed case and does not state the default position explicitly, but its examples chipánti, mipóquin, jismís, mapéti vs. jisi, mapeti presuppose a first/second-syllable window). Stress is assigned before coda-stop deletion, so a deleted coda still leaves its stress behind (opaque surface stress, written with an acute in headwords). Odd/even syllable counting also figures in the h-elision and h-shift rules (pp. 21).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.21 mentions 'un segundo proceso de acentuación' (a second stress process) making the sequence 'ia' in joshiaquin stressed, and p.19 calls the last unstressed syllable of a root 'weak' (débil), but no explicit secondary-stress rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None as lexical exceptions; the surface irregularities are all attributed to deleted coda stops/nasals (stress assigned before deletion), nasalization, silent j, and h-elision in even syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Capanahua as written in the ILV practical orthography (Loos's Capanahua of the Tapiche/Buncuya area); the copy read is the 2nd electronic edition (Lima: ILV, 2003) of the 1998 SLP 45 dictionary, whose p.15 pronunciation paragraph is word-for-word identical with the Rosetta Project scan of the 1998 print edition.

sources.quote: Another language in which Weight-to-Stress apparently applies only to a foot-bound heavy syllable is Capanahua, a language of Peru. The following is a summary of the relevant facts, taken from Loos 1969; the same data are found in Safir 1979. According to Loos 1969, Capanahua has both stress and high tone. These have distinct but predictable distributions which differ as follows. Stress occurs on the second syllable if it is closed (i.e., heavy), otherwise it falls on the first syllable. High tone, like stress, occurs on the second syllable if it is closed but, unlike stress, it falls on each of the first two syllables if the second syllable is not closed. [p.212] ... Monosyllables lack stress and high tone [p.212]
sources.note: Second-hand (from Loos 1969 and Safir 1979): one stress per word, on the second syllable if closed, else on the first; monosyllables (clitics ta?, ra?, ris and pronouns ?in, min, han) unstressed and toneless; high tone on the stressed syllable spreading rightward within the foot. Analysis: syllabic feet built iteratively L-to-R (evidence = every-other-syllable glottal deletion, following Safir 1979), Weight-to-Stress applies once per word within the first foot (heavy = consonant-final). fn.10: words with both first and second syllables heavy untested in Loos's data.
